people.label: Sean Michael Kirkpatrick
people.sub: First Director, AARO (Jul 2022-Dec 2023); DIA Chief Scientist; now CTO Defense & Intelligence, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
people.narrative: Kirkpatrick is the single most consequential figure in the containment architecture. A laser and materials physicist (BS 1991, PhD 1995, University of Georgia), he came to AARO through the exact channels that would matter: the National Reconnaissance Office and CIA Directorate of Science and Technology 2003-2007, then the Defense Intelligence Agency 2007-2016 as Chief Technology Officer, Division Chief and Defense Intelligence Officer for Scientific and Technical Intelligence, then deputy director of intelligence roles at US Strategic Command and US Space Command, with a stint on the National Security Council 2017-2018 as Director of National Security Strategy. He was named the first director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office when Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks established it by memorandum on 15 July 2022. He testified before the Senate Armed Services Emerging Threats and Capabilities Subcommittee on 19 April 2023 that AARO held over 650 cases and that spherical objects made up nearly half of them. He then became the public face of the Department's response to David Grusch: within days of the 26 July 2023 House Oversight hearing he posted on LinkedIn that the hearing was 'insulting' to the workforce, prompting the White House to publicly distance itself from him. He announced his departure on 7 November 2023 and left on 1 December 2023, and immediately took the job of Chief Technology Officer for Defense and Intelligence Programs at Oak Ridge National Laboratory - a laboratory operated by UT-Battelle that had supported AARO during his tenure, and which in 2024 was given custody of the alleged UAP material sample AARO analysed. On 19 January 2024 he published an op-ed in Scientific American arguing the whole disclosure record was 'a textbook example of circular reporting' traceable to 'a small group of interconnected believers' seeded by Robert Bigelow and AATIP. He shaped, then supervised the rollout of, the Historical Record Report Volume I, released 8 March 2024 after he had already left. In September 2025 he told the New York Post that Rep. Anna Paulina Luna's oversight was 'playhouse politics' and that the congressional UAP hearings were 'a disgrace' and 'reality TV'; Luna's office called him 'a known documented liar' who 'blocked the release of information' and 'tried to discredit witnesses.' By May 2026 his own successor, Jon Kosloski, had - per Luna - apologised to members of Congress for the conduct of the prior AARO leadership.

people.label: Jon T. Kosloski
people.sub: Director, AARO since 26 Aug 2024; former NSA quantum optics / cryptanalysis researcher
people.narrative: Kosloski is the third person to run AARO and the first whose tenure produced anything the disclosure side counts as movement. He came from the National Security Agency, where he was a senior research scientist working in quantum optics, cryptanalysis and advanced research; DoD announced his selection on 26 August 2024, ending nine months in which the office had no confirmed director. His public line is materially identical to Kirkpatrick's on the central question - 'to date, AARO has discovered no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology,' as he told the Senate Armed Services Emerging Threats and Capabilities Subcommittee on 19 November 2024 - but his framing diverges in two ways that matter. He has repeatedly conceded that a residue of cases is 'truly anomalous' and that there are cases he does not understand, and he has committed the office to declassification and data-sharing rather than pure debunking. At his 14 November 2024 media roundtable on the FY2024 report he disclosed the GREMLIN prototype sensor system undergoing a 90-day collection at a classified national security site, described AARO as employing several dozen personnel, and promised Volume II of the Historical Record Report 'within months' - a promise that as of August 2026 remains unkept. In May 2026 he met Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Tim Burchett and, per Luna, apologised for the conduct of the prior AARO leadership - after which Luna, who had spent more than a year demanding the office be defunded, publicly backed him. That apology is the closest thing to an institutional admission that the Kirkpatrick-era office behaved improperly toward Congress and witnesses.

entities.desc: Kona Blue was a Department of Homeland Security prospective special access programme, terminated on 10 February 2012, intended to house UAP recovery and reverse-engineering work after the DIA's AAWSAP/AATIP funding lapsed. AARO's framing is that Kona Blue was rejected by DHS leadership as lacking merit and that it is the proximate origin of the modern belief in a crash-retrieval programme - people who saw the Kona Blue proposal, on this account, mistook a proposal for an existing capability. A prospective special access programme is a real, chartered vehicle, and the surviving text discusses protection rationales for sensitive personnel and exotic technologies. The federal government did not draft a SAP charter to house nothing; it drafted one because named officials with clearances believed there was something to house, and the charter reached the Acting Deputy Secretary level of DHS before it was killed. AARO uses Kona Blue as a debunking device; on its face it is documentary evidence that in 2011-2012 senior officials at two departments treated recovered exotic material as a programme-management problem.

entities.sub: 9-page unclassified assessment; 144 incidents, 143 unexplained
entities.desc: The Preliminary Assessment delivered to Congress on 25 June 2021 under Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines is the founding public document of the modern era. It was mandated by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's directive accompanying the FY2021 intelligence authorisation and was drafted on the UAP Task Force's dataset: 144 reports from US government sources between 2004 and 2021, of which the assessment could explain exactly one. It declined to attribute the remainder, sorting possible explanations into airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, US industry developmental programmes, foreign adversary systems, and a catch-all 'other' bin that it said would require additional scientific advances to characterise. It conceded that in 18 incidents, observers reported unusual movement patterns or flight characteristics, and that some UAP appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, manoeuvre abruptly, or move at considerable speed without discernible means of propulsion. Its analytic move - that limited and inconsistent data prevents conclusions - became the permanent template for every AARO annual report that followed. Read as containment, the assessment is a masterpiece of bounded honesty: it conceded everything about the phenomenon and nothing about the government's history with it, and it said nothing whatever about recovery, materials or reverse engineering, which were outside its stated scope.

aaro.desc: AARO's structural problem, stated plainly: it is the only body with department-wide UAP cognizance, it has no subpoena power, no authority to compel contractor records, no independent counsel, no dedicated press function for most of its existence, and it reports to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. The DoD Inspector General found in DODIG-2023-109 that DoD components are not even required to report UAP incidents to it. Every negative finding AARO has published is therefore bounded twice over - by what a voluntary feed delivered, and by what an office inside OSD was willing to conclude about OSD. This is why the denial formula never varies and never widens: 'AARO has discovered no verifiable evidence' is literally true and answers nothing. The office's three directors have differed in tone, not in that sentence. What changed in 2026 was not AARO but the Department around it: a presidential direction, a cabinet-level declassification programme, an external science council, an abolition bill, and a subcommittee chair with a records demand.
